questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=(-2,0)\times {2,3}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=(-2,0)\times {2,3}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(-2,0)$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $2$ or $3.$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in (-2,0),\,y\in {2,3}}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(-2,0)$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $2$

$$
{S}_{1}={(x,2)\,:\,x\in (-2,0)}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/3ff59491671c85c444afefb827c5b7cc30d617547e88f8c87b0b7edb07c5ce90.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(-2,0)$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $3$

$$
{S}_{2}={(x,3)\,:\,x\in (-2,0)}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/45f703cae4149be4cc973c0537a7bb4c5fcd06b5bf3e1989004d762839154112.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/b501bc9b634b38c5b0f77fc7cd4e846208076014a83029428786e36488839999.png)

questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{3}].$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}={0.5}\times [0,0.125]={(0.5,k)\,:\,k\in [0,0.125]}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(0.5,0)$ to the point $(0.5,0.125)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/3a1bb7a7c54718e39df80092243a119ec8b5a6e77ec4f9d58ffb074e50191d04.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{3}]={(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,{i}^{3}]}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,{i}^{3}).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/472b6456019a5c89e585f80aa4a0dfd44f3b87c0624c10ea7b52f32e958a8c4e.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following figure that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/204c9a31031534ac70a599322c3f77a077440300fde2364476643c88406e34cd.png)

questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{2}].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have

$$
{X}_{1}={1}\times [0,{1}^{2}]={(1,k)\,:\,k\in [0,1]}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(1,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/6b6a47e464623fe9c572a52f7c71377136e68f41dcfd641920634b415568d7f5.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{2}]={(i,{k}^{2})\,:\,k\in [0,i]}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,{i}^{2}).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/c67cd0b545f0fc779d2977e38fab8164eb3b0161a18e32a615c71d88d1c30b68.png)

There are no points that lie in all sets. Therefore, the intersection of the indexed sets is $∅,$ the empty set.

canonical_examples.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $S = \{1, 2\} \times (0, 1)$ in the Cartesian plane.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \{1,2\} \times (0,1)
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $1$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \{{\color{red}{1}},{\color{blue}{2}}\},\, y\in (0,1) \Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ ({\color{red}{1}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \Big\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/56f200fce557749a56b9b5b51bc670da5f8c7f2cdb0196392ee80efcd6be980a.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_2 = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{2}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \big\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/f96074cc265bba6eb59717364d2aa5390fdccea4d398fe5ae0b99f7ad82f0b93.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S = S_1\cup S_2
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/0c0529aaa680b4b572d17f2cfbfb76d805134e72c50ab3ed469286cc025185a3.png)

S = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z,\, y\in \mathbb N\Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}.$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ (x, {\color{red}{1}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/6b63e973bbcc3e25d601a1f6cef97f5a00cc22e738c46d04a1ac06851421894e.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

$$
S_2 = \Big\{ (x,{\color{blue}{2}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_2$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/f24ce8f7610d096c795a8a74b0b714b720c36442042c28b66432d6b2102fb9d4.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3,S_4,S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup {S}_{4}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/c999c61d8ffbb27d47272811e32340cef3253b4730e684be10615487a8b27200.png)

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
canonical_examples.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $\,\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} X_i$ in the Cartesian plane given that $I = [-1,1] \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $X_i = \{ i \} \times [0, \, i^2].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x \: : \: x \in A_k \:\:\textrm{for at least one}\:\: k \in I \big\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=-0.5,$ we have 

$$
X_{-0.5} = \{ -0.5 \} \times [0, 0.25] = \big\{ (-0.5,k) \: : \: k \in [0, 0.25] \big\}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(-0.5, 0)$ to the point $(-0.5,0.25)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/ccc75eac899efcab1d0b6fde12609a3ea8f61d6fec74c739ef3393fad32645a9.png)

In general,

$$
X_i = \{ i \} \times [0, i^2] = \big\{ (i,k) \: : \: k \in [0, i^2] \big\}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i, i^2).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/60c98be5d97748e9285bb5e9c30bba9781a5ef99245789718a7828b18a6df8fb.png)

 

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following figure that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} X_i{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/b3a61d686c78c76a4f461c1c771437d31030339b634661da8b8dc4f492db55eb.png)
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Visualizing Intersections of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
canonical_examples.problem: Let $I = [0,1] \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $X_i = [-i, 0] \times [-1,1].$ Sketch a representation of $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i \in I} X_i$ in the Cartesian plane.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x \: : \: x \in A_k \:\:\textrm{for all}\:\: k \in I \big\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
X_{0.5} = [-0.5,0] \times [-1, 1] = \big\{ (a,b) \: : \: a \in [-0.5, 0], b \in [-1, 1] \big\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(-0.5, -1),$ $(-0.5, 1),$ $(0, 1),$ and $(0, -1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/8ad650cb3f2fa4da920a442e8cc1b24af5027595cba4e43138eff2126cf4c102.png)

In general,

$$
X_i = [-i, 0] \times [-1,1] = \big\{ (a,b) \: : \: a \in [-i, 0], b \in [-1, 1] \big\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(-i,-1),$ $(-i,1),$ $(0, 1),$ and $(0, -1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/a37cfa508cf3a60536084fbc1e57c5aeac3414904d2ad72ef1deda85dc4eddd8.png)

 

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $\{0\}\times [-1,1]{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/5e9a611629f4370c57e77a057439c759670afa17c14c4b2339e1d471f616ea72.png)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that if $A$ and $B$ are sets, the Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/e74fb5948144bc61173e4de73865cb746278bd31fd87e4abf927fa01821ba936.png)

tutorials.name: Cartesian Products of Countably Infinite Sets
tutorials.problem:
Cartesian coordinates can also be used to visualize other Cartesian products.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/033c40b86bfd5cebf24d34de644f632213207386c2b67c559af7594468599e1e.png)

tutorials.name: The Cartesian Product [0,1] x [0,1]
tutorials.problem:
Let's sketch a representation of the set $S= [0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the Cartesian plane.

The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S = [0,1] \times [0, 1]
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=
\big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in [0,1],\, y\in [0,1] \big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_0 \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}0}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{red}0} = \big\{ ({\color{red}{0}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

We can represent $S_{\color{red}0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general $S_{\color{blue}{i}} \subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S_{\color{blue}{i}} = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{i}},y) \: : \: y \in [0,1]\big\}
$$

For each ${\color{blue}{i}} \in [0,1],$ $S_{\color{blue}{i}}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $({\color{blue}{i}},0)$ to the point $({\color{blue}{i}},1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/28b9aa0559635ed4090f10dd0b59f2cbb6c297f8736d9509a637b5d78d27561c.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I = [0,1]{:}$

$$
S = \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}.
$$

As $\color{blue}i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union $\displaystyle \bigcup_{{\color{blue}i} \in I} S_{\color{blue}i}{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124149/assets/76ff48755dbfc3ba1943665d08aa8cfd00948bbc1ddfaab560a0af64f11bae26.png)
